name: CI/CD & Pipelines
description: Continuous integration, deployment strategies, pipeline design, artefacts and release safety.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What CI/CD & Pipelines is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is continuous integration (CI)?
cards.answer: Merging every developer's changes into the shared main branch frequently — at least daily — with an automated pipeline that builds the code and runs the tests on every change, so integration problems surface within minutes.
cards.explanation: Before CI, teams merged weeks of separate work at once and spent days untangling conflicts ("integration hell"). A red CI build is treated as the team's top priority to fix.

cards.prompt: Continuous delivery vs continuous deployment
cards.answer: Both keep every change releasable. Continuous delivery means any change that passes the pipeline could be deployed with one click; continuous deployment means it is deployed to production automatically.

right.title: Continuous deployment
points: Needs excellent automated tests and monitoring

cards.explanation: The "CD" in CI/CD can mean either. Both rely on the same foundations: automated tests, repeatable builds and safe deployment techniques.

cards.prompt: What is a CI/CD pipeline?
cards.answer: An automated sequence of stages that every change passes through — typically checkout, build, test, security scans, package, then deploy to staging and production — defined as code in the repository.
cards.explanation: If any stage fails, the pipeline stops and reports, so broken changes never reach users. Popular platforms: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI, Azure Pipelines.

cards.prompt: What is a build artifact?
cards.answer: The output a pipeline produces and later deploys — a container image, a JAR, a compiled binary, a bundle of static files — stored with a version so the exact same thing can be deployed to every environment.
cards.explanation: "Build once, deploy many": building a fresh artifact for production risks shipping something different from what was tested in staging.

cards.prompt: What are development, staging and production environments?
cards.answer: Development is where engineers build and experiment; staging is a production-like copy used for final checks; production is the live system real users depend on.
cards.explanation: The closer staging matches production — same configuration, versions and similar data — the more its test results mean. Production data and credentials should never be used casually in lower environments.

modules.name: CI, CD and Pipeline Design
modules.description: What the terms mean, and what a good pipeline actually does.

cards.prompt: Distinguish continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment.
cards.answer: CI: everyone merges to trunk frequently and every merge is built and tested. Continuous delivery: every green build is *releasable* and deployment is a button. Continuous deployment: every green build ships to production automatically.
cards.explanation: CI is a team practice, not a tool — running Jenkins while sitting on week-old branches is not CI. The prerequisite for the last step is confidence: fast reliable tests, feature flags, monitoring, and a rollback that works.

cards.prompt: What stages belong in a solid pipeline, and in what order?
cards.answer: Lint and type-check → unit tests → build once and produce an immutable artefact → integration tests → security scans (SCA/SAST) → deploy to staging → smoke and end-to-end tests → deploy to production → post-deploy verification.
cards.explanation: Two rules matter most: fail fast (cheapest checks first) and build once, promote the same artefact through every environment. Rebuilding per environment means the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped.

cards.prompt: Why should configuration differ per environment while the artefact does not?
cards.answer: So the binary or image tested in staging is byte-identical to the one in production. Environment differences live in injected configuration and secrets, never in a rebuild.
cards.explanation: This is why images are tagged by commit SHA rather than `latest`, and promoted by re-tagging. `latest` is unpinnable, unrollbackable and non-reproducible — the single most common source of 'it worked yesterday'.

cards.prompt: Your pipeline fails randomly about 10% of the time. Why is that worse than it sounds?
cards.answer: Flaky tests destroy the signal: people re-run until green, so real failures get ignored too. Quarantine flaky tests immediately, track them as bugs, and fix the root cause — usually timing, shared state, ordering or real concurrency bugs.
cards.explanation: A 10% flake rate across 20 independent jobs means most runs fail somewhere. Automatic retries hide the symptom and let it spread. Note that a flaky test sometimes indicates a genuine race in the product — the test is right and the code is wrong.

cards.prompt: How should a pipeline handle secrets and credentials?
cards.answer: Short-lived credentials via OIDC federation instead of stored long-lived keys; secrets scoped per environment; masked in logs; never exposed to workflows triggered by untrusted forks; and least-privilege tokens per job.
cards.explanation: CI is a high-value target — it can push to production and holds every credential. Pin third-party actions to a commit SHA, since a mutable tag lets a compromised action run in your pipeline with your secrets.

resources.title: GitHub Docs — Security hardening for GitHub Actions

modules.name: Deployment Strategies
modules.description: Getting changes into production without taking it down.

cards.prompt: Blue-green vs canary deployment
cards.answer: Blue-green switches all traffic between two complete environments; canary shifts a small percentage first and increases it while watching metrics.

left.title: Blue-green
points: All users hit the new version at once

right.title: Canary
points: Blast radius limited to a few percent
Needs traffic routing and good telemetry

cards.explanation: Rolling updates are the default in Kubernetes and sit between the two. Whichever you pick, the database is the hard part: schema changes must be backwards compatible so old and new code can run simultaneously.

cards.prompt: How do feature flags decouple deploy from release, and what is the cost?
cards.answer: Code ships dark and is enabled per user, percentage or environment — so a bad feature is switched off without a redeploy. The cost is complexity: every flag doubles the paths through your system, and stale flags rot.
cards.explanation: Treat flags as inventory with an owner and an expiry date. Test the on and off paths. Kill switches for risky dependencies are the highest-value flags; long-lived permanent flags usually mean a configuration option in disguise.

cards.prompt: A deploy is causing errors. Roll back or fix forward?
cards.answer: Roll back first, diagnose after — unless the change included an irreversible migration, in which case fix forward. The decision must be made before the incident, and rollback must be practised.
cards.explanation: This is why migrations are expand/contract: never drop a column in the same release that stops writing it. An untested rollback is not a rollback; rehearse it in staging, and know how long it takes.

cards.prompt: What is GitOps?
cards.answer: Git holds the declarative desired state of the system, and an in-cluster agent (Argo CD, Flux) continuously reconciles the cluster toward it. Deployments happen by merging, not by running commands.
cards.explanation: The wins are a full audit trail, review on infrastructure changes, drift detection and revert-by-git. The trap is secrets — they cannot sit in plain git, so you need sealed secrets, SOPS or an external secrets operator.

modules.name: Pipeline Engineering
modules.description: Caching, matrices, merge queues, environments and approvals, migrations, release automation, signing and preview environments.

cards.prompt: How do you make CI fast without making it unreliable?
cards.answer: Cache dependency downloads keyed on the lockfile hash, cache build outputs where the tool supports it (remote build caches), run independent jobs in parallel, run only affected tests in monorepos, and fail fast with cheap checks first.
cards.explanation: A cache must be keyed on everything that affects its contents; a stale cache that restores the wrong dependencies causes baffling failures. Treat CI duration as a product metric — a 40-minute pipeline changes how often people integrate.

resources.title: GitHub Docs — Caching dependencies to speed up workflows

cards.prompt: What is a build matrix, and when is it worth the cost?
cards.answer: One job definition expanded over combinations of variables — operating systems, runtime versions, database versions — each run in parallel. It is worth it for libraries and tools that promise support for several platforms or versions.
cards.explanation: Applications usually need only their production target plus the next upgrade. Keep matrices small and meaningful: every cell multiplies CI minutes and flake exposure. Use `fail-fast: false` when you want the full picture of which combinations break.

resources.title: GitHub Docs — Running variations of jobs in a workflow

cards.prompt: Two pull requests each pass CI, are merged minutes apart, and main is now broken. How can that happen, and what prevents it?
cards.answer: Each PR was tested against an older main, not against main plus the other PR — semantic conflicts that merge cleanly as text still break. A merge queue tests each PR on top of the current main plus everything queued ahead of it, merging only when that combination passes.
cards.explanation: "Require branches to be up to date" also works but forces serial rebases that do not scale on busy repositories. Merge queues keep trunk green at high merge rates, which trunk-based development depends on.

resources.title: GitHub Docs — Managing a merge queue

cards.prompt: What should protect deployments to production in a pipeline?
cards.answer: Deployment environments with their own secrets, required reviewers or approval rules where appropriate, restrictions on which branches may deploy, wait timers or change windows if the business needs them, and an audit log of who deployed what and when.
cards.explanation: Scope production credentials to the production environment so a workflow run from a feature branch or a fork can never obtain them. Automated gates (tests, security scans, SLO checks) are preferable to manual approval as the main safety mechanism.

resources.title: GitHub Docs — Managing environments for deployment

cards.prompt: Where do database migrations run in a deployment pipeline, and what must be true of them?
cards.answer: As an explicit step before the new code is rolled out (a job or init container that runs once, not every pod racing at startup). Each migration must be backwards compatible with the code currently running — expand first, deploy code, contract later — so old and new versions can coexist during the rollout.
cards.explanation: Destructive changes (drop, rename, type change) go in a later release, after no running code depends on the old shape. Keep migrations small, run them against a production-sized copy first, and set lock timeouts so a migration cannot freeze the database.

resources.title: Prisma Data Guide — Expand and contract pattern

cards.prompt: How can versioning and changelogs be automated?
cards.answer: Derive the next version from commit messages (Conventional Commits: `fix:` → patch, `feat:` → minor, `!` or `BREAKING CHANGE` → major) with tools such as semantic-release, release-please or Changesets, which also generate the changelog, tag the release and publish packages.
cards.explanation: Automation removes the "who bumps the version?" step and keeps changelogs honest, but only if commit and PR titles follow the convention — enforce them with a lint check. For applications deployed continuously, a commit SHA is often all the version you need.

cards.prompt: What do artifact signing and provenance add to a pipeline?
cards.answer: Signing (for example Sigstore cosign, keyless via the CI's OIDC identity) proves an image or package came from your pipeline and was not altered. Provenance attestations (SLSA) record how it was built — source commit, builder, inputs — so deployers can verify policy before running it.
cards.explanation: Admission controllers or deployment steps can then refuse unsigned or unattested artifacts, so a stolen registry credential alone cannot push something that will run. Pair with SBOMs to know what is inside every artifact.

resources.title: SLSA — Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts

cards.prompt: What are preview (ephemeral) environments, and what do they cost?
cards.answer: A short-lived deployment for each pull request, with its own URL, so reviewers, designers and QA can try the change before it merges. Destroyed automatically when the PR closes.
cards.explanation: They shorten feedback loops dramatically for front-end and product work. Costs: infrastructure per open PR, seeding realistic but safe data (never production personal data), and handling shared dependencies such as databases and third-party sandboxes.
